process-engineer.name: Process Engineer
process-engineer.short: Engineers who set up, improve and keep stable the front-end steps, such as deposition, etching and lithography, that build transistors and wiring on the wafer.
process-engineer.description: What a semiconductor process engineer does: developing recipes for front-end steps, improving them and keeping production stable, plus the skills and fields to study.

sections.p: Process engineers own the front-end steps that build transistors and wiring on the wafer, such as deposition, etching, lithography, ion implantation and CMP. In many fabs, each engineer is responsible for one step or a small group of steps. The core of the job is developing the tool settings (the recipe) that give the target film thickness, dimensions and profile, and then watching for drift during volume production so that quality holds. When the measurement data looks abnormal, they find the cause and decide on a fix. When a new product or process is introduced, they plan experiments and work to widen the process window.

sections.h: Who they work with and what they handle
sections.p: Day-to-day work involves equipment engineers, process engineers on neighboring steps, integration engineers who own the overall flow, and yield and quality engineers. What they handle: the production tools and their recipes, metrology data such as film thickness and critical dimensions, defect inspection results, and control charts for their step. How their time is split between the cleanroom, checking tools and wafers, and the office, analyzing data and writing reports, varies by company and by step.

The foundation is understanding the physics and chemistry of your step, whether that is plasma, chemical reactions, thin films or optics. On top of that, statistics for handling variation is essential: you need to use SPC (statistical process control) and design of experiments to find out what really matters with as few experiments as possible. Because a change in one step affects the steps before and after it and the electrical results, knowing the transistor structure and the whole process flow lets you isolate causes faster. Being able to organize data and explain it clearly to other teams matters too.

Start with the “The fabrication process” course to get the whole flow from bare wafer to wiring. Then go deeper into the fields for the steps you are likely to own: “Lithography” and “Etching” for patterning, “Deposition (CVD and PVD)” for films, “CMP and cleaning” for planarization and cleaning, and “Ion implantation” and “Oxidation and diffusion” for doping. The statistics used to control a process are in “Yield and quality control”, and the ways to check results are in “Metrology and analysis”. If semiconductors are completely new to you, begin with the “Semiconductors for beginners” course.

faq.q: Can I become a process engineer without a science or engineering background?
faq.a: In general, most openings for this role expect knowledge of chemistry, physics, materials or electrical engineering. That said, some companies hire people from other fields or without industry experience and train them on the job. Hiring requirements differ by company and change over time, so check each job posting. Learning the principles of the process steps and basic statistics on your own will make your first months much easier.

faq.q: How is it different from an equipment engineer?
faq.a: Broadly, the process engineer is responsible for what is done to the wafer and how (the recipe and its result), and the equipment engineer is responsible for keeping the tool running correctly (maintenance and installation). In practice the boundary overlaps, and the two often investigate together whether a problem comes from the tool or from the recipe. How the roles are divided varies by company.

faq.q: Do I need any license or certification?
faq.a: In general, no specific license or certification is required to become a process engineer. Some workplaces provide internal training on handling chemicals and gases safely, or encourage related qualifications depending on the materials and facilities involved. Understanding of the process physics, statistics and the ability to reason from data usually count for more than certificates.

equipment-engineer.name: Equipment Engineer
equipment-engineer.short: Engineers who keep fab tools running to specification through maintenance, troubleshooting and tool installation. Some work in chipmakers' fabs; others work for equipment makers supporting customer fabs.
equipment-engineer.description: What a semiconductor equipment engineer does: maintaining, troubleshooting and installing fab tools, how it differs from field service, and the fields to study first.

sections.p: Equipment engineers keep the cleanroom's tools, such as deposition, etch, lithography and cleaning tools and the wafer handling systems, running to specification. The main tasks are planned preventive maintenance such as part replacement and chamber cleaning, troubleshooting to bring a tool that is down back into production, and installing new tools from delivery through to performance qualification. Because tool uptime directly limits how much a fab can produce, analyzing failure trends and preventing recurrence is just as important. Besides working in a chipmaker's fab, some engineers work as field service engineers for an equipment maker, installing and maintaining tools at customer sites.

sections.h: Who they work with and what they handle
sections.p: In the fab they work daily with process engineers, who set the recipes, and with production staff who run the tools. They also deal often with engineers from equipment makers who supply parts and service. What they handle: vacuum pumps, RF generators that create the plasma, mass flow controllers (MFC) that meter the gases, electrostatic chucks that hold the wafer, wafer handling robots and other parts, along with the logs and alarms the tool records. Some tools use toxic or flammable specialty gases and chemicals, so following safety procedures is a precondition of the job.

A tool combines mechanics, electrical systems, vacuum, control and chemistry, so broad fundamentals help: the basics of vacuum and plasma, electrical circuits and control, gas lines and gas handling, and how to read tool logs. Troubleshooting calls for logical isolation, narrowing the possible causes from the symptoms and checking them one by one. Before any work, a firm habit of following the safety basics is essential, such as lockout/tagout (LOTO) to isolate energy sources so the tool cannot start unexpectedly, and checking the SDS (safety data sheet) for the materials involved.

Start with the “Cleanrooms and equipment” and “Environment, health and safety” fields to cover the fab environment and the basics of safety. Then, depending on the tools you are likely to handle, study “Etching”, “Deposition (CVD and PVD)” and “Lithography”: knowing what a tool is for makes conversations with process engineers much easier. The gases and chemicals tools use are in “Process materials (gases and chemicals)”, and the ways to check tool condition and results are in “Metrology and analysis”. The “The fabrication process” course walks through the whole flow.

faq.q: Can I become an equipment engineer without a technical background or industry experience?
faq.a: In general, mechanical, electrical and electronics knowledge is useful for this role, and people who did facility or machine maintenance in other industries sometimes move into it using that experience. Some companies hire people without industry experience and train them internally, but hiring requirements differ by company and change over time. Learning basic circuits, vacuum and safety thinking will help you get up to speed faster.

faq.q: How does an equipment engineer at a chipmaker differ from field service at an equipment maker?
faq.a: An equipment engineer at a chipmaker keeps many kinds of tools in their own fab running so production does not stop. A field service engineer at an equipment maker is a specialist in that company's own tools and installs, starts up, maintains and repairs them at customer fabs, which usually means working on site at the customers they support. The details of the work vary by company.

faq.q: Do I need any license or certification?
faq.a: In general, no specific license or certification is required to become an equipment engineer. However, depending on the facilities, gases and type of work, laws or company rules may require specific training or qualifications. What is required differs by country and workplace, so check with the team you join.

yield-engineer.name: Yield and Quality Engineer
yield-engineer.short: Engineers who raise the share of good chips per wafer (yield) by tracking down the causes of failures through data and analysis, and turn them into process improvements and stable quality.
yield-engineer.description: What a yield and quality engineer does: yield analysis, defect data, SPC process control and failure analysis, who they work with, and the fields and terms to study.

sections.p: Yield and quality engineers raise yield, the share of good chips from each wafer, and keep quality stable. They combine wafer test results, data from defect inspection systems, metrology from each step and tool processing history to find where and why failures were created. For example, if failing chips cluster in one region of the wafer, a particular tool or step becomes a suspect. Once the candidates are narrowed down, they confirm the cause with physical analysis and agree on countermeasures with the owners of the steps involved. In volume production, another key role is using SPC (statistical process control) to catch process shifts early and build systems that prevent failures.

sections.h: Who they work with and what they handle
sections.p: Most causes lie in the process or the tools, so they investigate together with process engineers, equipment engineers and integration engineers. They also work with test engineers, who own the test results, failure analysis teams, who do the physical analysis, and quality assurance, who handle customers when problems appear after shipment. What they handle is large amounts of data: the distribution of failures across the wafer (wafer maps), defect locations and images, control charts and lot processing histories. Physical analysis includes, for example, cutting a cross-section with an FIB (focused ion beam) and imaging it with an SEM or TEM (transmission electron microscope).

Statistics and data analysis are at the center. You need to be comfortable with variation, with telling correlation from causation, and with control charts and the process capability index (Cpk). Because the data volumes are large, some workplaces use database queries and programming languages for analysis in addition to spreadsheets. On top of that, understanding each process step and the structure of transistors and wiring lets you connect a data anomaly to a physical cause. When the cause is not obvious, persistence in forming hypotheses and checking them one at a time is essential.

Start with the “Yield and quality control” field to learn how yield is defined, how defect density relates to chip area, and quality tools such as control charts. Ways to confirm a failure's cause are in “Metrology and analysis”, how test results are produced is in “Testing and inspection”, and the failure mechanisms that matter after shipment are in “Reliability”. For the process itself, take the “The fabrication process” course; for test and reliability in the back end, take “Back end, quality and safety”. “Lithography” and “Etching” come up especially often when thinking about pattern defects.

faq.q: Can I become a yield and quality engineer without a technical background or industry experience?
faq.a: Statistics and data analysis are central to this role, so people with quality control or data analysis experience from other industries can find their skills useful. On the other hand, linking a data anomaly to a cause in the process takes knowledge of semiconductor processes and devices. Hiring requirements differ by company and change over time, but learning basic statistics and the process flow makes the role easier to enter from either side.

faq.q: How is it different from quality assurance?
faq.a: In general, yield and quality engineers focus on reducing failures inside the fab and stabilizing the process. Quality assurance guarantees that products meet specifications and customer requirements, and when problems appear after shipment, it often handles explanations to customers and coordinates the prevention of recurrence. The two are closely linked, and the titles and division of roles vary by company.

faq.q: Do I need any license or certification?
faq.a: In general, no specific license or certification is required for this role. Some people use certificates in quality control or statistics as a study goal, but how much they count in hiring differs by company. In practice, experience in tracking down causes from data and working with others to deliver improvements usually counts most.

device-engineer.name: Device Engineer
device-engineer.short: Engineers who design the structure of transistors and other devices, measure and evaluate the electrical characteristics of prototypes, and turn them into models for circuit design.
device-engineer.description: What a device engineer does: transistor development, electrical characterization, TCAD simulation and SPICE models, plus the knowledge and fields to study first.

sections.p: Device engineers shape the structure and characteristics of transistors and other devices so they deliver the intended performance. They set targets for threshold voltage, on-current, leakage current and so on, and work out how the dopant profiles and gate structure should change to meet them. On prototype wafers they measure current-voltage and capacitance characteristics and investigate gaps from the targets and the sources of variation. During development they may also use TCAD (process and device simulation) to predict characteristics before building anything. The measured characteristics are condensed into SPICE models that are handed to circuit designers.

sections.h: Who they work with and what they handle
sections.p: Because device structure is set by the process, they work closely with integration engineers, who own the overall flow, and with process engineers. They also exchange information with circuit designers who use the models and with reliability engineers who study long-term degradation. What they handle: evaluation patterns built on the wafer (test structures, often called TEGs in Japan and test keys in Taiwan), probers and instruments that contact and measure them, measurement data and simulation results. The devices they work on vary by company, from logic and memory transistors to power semiconductors, sensors and compound semiconductors.

The foundation is semiconductor physics, PN junctions and how a MOSFET works. You should be able to explain mobility, depletion layers, short-channel effects and the like with both equations and diagrams. Electrical characterization requires not only knowing the instruments but also spotting parasitic resistance and capacitance and measurement errors. Programming helps with modeling and data handling, and if you use TCAD, the ability to interpret its results physically is important. Process knowledge lets you link a change in characteristics to a change in structure, and knowing how circuit designers use the models helps you judge how accurate they need to be.

Start with the “Understanding devices” course and build the basics in order: “Semiconductor physics”, “PN junctions and diodes”, then “MOSFET”. If you will work on scaled transistors, “Advanced transistors (FinFET and GAA)” covers the structures used to suppress short-channel effects. Device degradation is in “Reliability”, and if you will handle power applications, “Power semiconductors” is useful. Evaluation methods are also covered in “Metrology and analysis”. As you work through the questions in each field, check whether you can explain terms such as threshold voltage and mobility in your own words.

faq.q: Can I become a device engineer without a science or engineering background?
faq.a: This role often demands strong specialist knowledge of semiconductor physics and electronics. In general, people who studied electrical engineering, physics or materials are the usual candidates, and going straight in from a non-technical background is not easy. Hiring requirements do differ by company and change over time, though, and building experience in a related role first and moving over later is a possible path.

faq.q: How is it different from a circuit designer?
faq.a: Device engineers shape the structure and characteristics of individual transistors and capture those characteristics in models. Circuit designers use those models to combine transistors into circuits with the functions they need. Because device performance drives circuit performance, the two discuss characteristic targets and model accuracy as they work.

faq.q: Do I need any license or certification?
faq.a: In general, no specific license or certification is required. What counts is understanding how semiconductor devices work and experience with measurement and simulation. As a student, measuring device characteristics or running simulations in classes or research is good preparation that is close to the actual work.

integration-engineer.name: Process Integration Engineer
integration-engineer.short: Engineers who link many process steps into a manufacturing flow that makes the device work as intended overall. They play a central role when new technology generations and products are introduced.
integration-engineer.description: What a process integration engineer does: designing the process flow, evaluating test structures and introducing new nodes and products, plus the fields to study.

sections.p: Chip manufacturing is a long sequence that repeats deposition, lithography, etching, ion implantation and other steps many times. Process integration engineers design this whole flow and make sure that when the individual steps are combined, the device reaches its target characteristics and yield. Changing the conditions of one step affects the steps around it and the electrical results, so they look at the whole and choose the best combination. When a new technology generation or a new product is introduced, they set the step sequence and targets, evaluate the prototype results and bring the process to the point where it can move into volume production.

sections.h: Who they work with and what they handle
sections.p: It is a role that often sits between the process engineers for each step, device engineers who shape the characteristics, yield and quality engineers and the design teams, acting as the coordinator. What they handle: the process flow describing the order and conditions of the steps, test structures built on the wafer and their electrical measurement results, cross-section images and yield data. They may also contribute to the design rules and the PDK (process design kit) given to designers. After volume production starts, they lead the work on yield and characteristic problems that span several steps.

Rather than deep expertise in a single step, the role calls for a broad understanding of the principles of every step and how they connect. A basic requirement is being able to picture the cross-section from STI (shallow trench isolation) through the transistor and silicide up to the wiring. You also need to infer which step is the likely cause from electrical measurement results. Because the job means pulling together the views of many teams and making decisions, the ability to explain logically with evidence and set priorities is important too.

Start with the “The fabrication process” course and work through the front-end fields in order. “Lithography”, “Etching”, “Deposition (CVD and PVD)”, “Ion implantation” and “Interconnect processes” are especially essential for building a flow. How the process affects device characteristics is covered in the “MOSFET” and “Advanced transistors (FinFET and GAA)” fields, or in the “Understanding devices” course. Finally, the “Yield and quality control” field covers how to think about evaluation on the way to volume production.

faq.q: Can I become a process integration engineer without a technical background or industry experience?
faq.a: The role draws on knowledge of both the whole process and devices, so in general a science or engineering background is usually expected. Some people take it on after working as process or device engineers, while others are assigned to it as new graduates; the approach varies by company. Either way, the starting point is a working understanding of each process step and the transistor structure.

faq.q: How is it different from a process engineer?
faq.a: A process engineer is responsible for the conditions and results of a specific step and goes deep into that step. A process integration engineer is responsible for the combination of steps as a whole and for the final device characteristics and yield. For example, the integration engineer may set the target for a dimension and the process engineer develops the recipe that achieves it, but the boundary varies by company.

faq.q: Do I need any license or certification?
faq.a: In general, no specific license or certification is required. Broad knowledge of process and devices, the ability to infer causes from data and the ability to coordinate many teams count most. Getting exposure to experiments or research involving semiconductor processing or devices as a student makes the job easier to picture.

reliability-engineer.name: Reliability Engineer
reliability-engineer.short: Engineers who verify and assure that products keep working without failure over their service life, using accelerated stress tests and analysis of failure mechanisms.
reliability-engineer.description: What a reliability engineer does: HTOL, THB, HAST and temperature cycling tests, failure mechanisms and lifetime models, plus the fields and terms to study first.

sections.p: Reliability engineers confirm that semiconductor products keep working without failure over their intended service life and operating environment. Since you cannot wait for the real service life to pass, they run accelerated tests that speed up degradation with higher temperature, voltage or humidity. Typical tests include HTOL (high-temperature operating life), THB (temperature-humidity-bias), HAST (highly accelerated stress test) and temperature cycling. They plan these tests and take part in qualification, the decision on whether a product can go into volume production and ship based on the results. When failures occur, they analyze the mechanism and feed it back into design or process improvements.

sections.h: Who they work with and what they handle
sections.p: Degradation can originate in the transistors, the wiring or the package, so they work with device engineers, process engineers, packaging engineers and circuit designers. When customers request reliability data or a problem occurs in the field, they may also respond together with quality assurance. What they handle: environmental chambers and test boards, test standards, analysis results for failed samples, and lifetime data with its statistical analysis. Test conditions are often based on industry standards such as JEDEC standards and, for automotive products, AEC-Q100.

Understanding failure mechanisms is at the core. Examples include electromigration, in which metal atoms in the wiring are moved by current; TDDB (time-dependent dielectric breakdown), in which the gate dielectric breaks down over time; NBTI and hot carrier injection (HCI), which shift the threshold voltage; and package failures caused by thermal strain. To translate accelerated test results to real use conditions, you need to be fluent with acceleration models such as the Arrhenius model and lifetime statistics such as the Weibull distribution. Reading standards precisely and recording and explaining conditions and results carefully is also expected.

Start with the “Reliability” field to learn the bathtub curve, how failure rates are expressed, the main failure mechanisms and the idea behind accelerated testing. If you will handle automotive products, “Automotive Semiconductors and Functional Safety” covers their quality requirements and standards. Because most failures occur in transistors, wiring or packages, also studying “MOSFET”, “Interconnect processes” and “Packaging and assembly” lets you reason about causes from the structure. The “Back end, quality and safety” course gives the overall picture from the back end through quality.

faq.q: Can I become a reliability engineer without a science or engineering background?
faq.a: Because you need to understand failure mechanisms physically, in general a background in electrical engineering, physics, materials or mechanical engineering is useful for this role. On the other hand, test planning, statistical analysis and standards-based management have a lot in common with reliability and quality work in other industries. Hiring requirements differ by company and change over time.

faq.q: How is it different from a yield and quality engineer?
faq.a: Yield and quality engineers focus on reducing parts that are already defective when they are made. Reliability engineers deal with whether parts that were good when shipped will fail during use. Both use failure analysis and statistics, but it helps to think of the difference as the time scale each one covers.

faq.q: Do I need any license or certification?
faq.a: In general, no specific license or certification is required. Some people use certificates in reliability engineering or quality control as study aids, but how much they count in hiring differs by company. In practice, understanding failure mechanisms, reading test standards correctly and judging results statistically count most.

test-engineer.name: Test Engineer
test-engineer.short: Engineers who develop the tests, run on automatic test equipment (ATE), that check whether chips work to specification at wafer level and after packaging, balancing quality against test cost.
test-engineer.description: What a test engineer does: ATE test programs, wafer and final test, working with designers on DFT and cutting test cost, plus the fields and terms to study first.

sections.p: Test engineers create the tests that check whether manufactured chips work to specification and make them ready for volume production. Testing is generally split into wafer test, done on the wafer before dicing, and final test, done after the chips are assembled into packages. They develop test programs that run on ATE (automatic test equipment), defining what to measure, such as voltages, currents, timing and functions, and the pass/fail limits. The real skill lies in reliably catching defective parts while shortening test time per chip to keep costs down. After volume production starts, they keep analyzing test results and improving the tests.

sections.h: Who they work with and what they handle
sections.p: What can be tested is decided by the chip's design, so they work with circuit designers from an early stage, especially those responsible for DFT (design for testability). Test results are also used for yield analysis, so they work with yield and quality engineers too. What they handle: the ATE, probe cards that touch needles to the pads on the wafer, fixtures and boards that connect the chip to the ATE, test programs, and large volumes of test result data. Besides in-house test operations, they may work with an OSAT that provides test services to bring a product into volume production.

You need the fundamentals of both digital and analog circuits. On the digital side, it helps to understand scan test, ATPG (automatic test pattern generation) and fault coverage; on the analog side, how to measure the characteristics of op-amps and ADCs. Programming skills for writing test programs, the ability to read datasheet specifications precisely, and the ability to spot measurement error and noise are also required. Test escapes lead to failures in the field while excessive testing raises cost, so the perspective of balancing the two is essential.

Start with the “Testing and inspection” field to cover the basics of wafer test, burn-in, scan test and so on. To understand what you are testing, study “Logic circuits”, “Analog and electronic circuits” and “A/D and D/A conversion”; you will see which parameters are measured and why. How to read specifications is in “How to read datasheets”, and how test results are used is in “Yield and quality control”. Among the courses, “Back end, quality and safety” and “Circuits, design and memory” are recommended.

faq.q: Can I become a test engineer without a technical background or industry experience?
faq.a: This role uses both circuit knowledge and programming, so in general people with electrical, electronics or computing knowledge tend to be the main candidates. Software development experience can be useful for developing test programs. Hiring requirements differ by company and change over time, but learning circuit basics and how testing works will help you understand the job faster.

faq.q: How is it different from a design verification engineer?
faq.a: Verification engineers check, before manufacturing, that the design itself meets the specification, mainly through simulation. Test engineers use equipment to check each manufactured chip for defects introduced during manufacturing. Put simply, the first finds design errors and the second finds manufacturing defects.

faq.q: Do I need any license or certification?
faq.a: In general, no specific license or certification is required to become a test engineer. In practice, understanding circuits, programming skills for writing test programs and the ability to analyze data and turn it into improvements count most. The ATE and programming environment differ by workplace and are usually learned on the job.

package-engineer.name: Packaging Engineer
package-engineer.short: Engineers who design packages and run the assembly processes that connect a chip to the outside world and protect it from heat, mechanical stress and moisture, including advanced packages that combine several chips.
package-engineer.description: What a packaging engineer does: package design and assembly, thermal and mechanical evaluation, and advanced packaging such as chiplets, plus the fields to study.

sections.p: Packaging engineers take chips cut from the wafer and turn them into a form that connects electrically to the board and protects them from heat, mechanical stress and moisture. The work broadly divides into design and development, deciding the package structure and materials, and assembly process engineering, developing and sustaining steps such as dicing, die bonding, wire bonding or flip-chip interconnection and encapsulation. They use simulation and evaluation to check how heat will be removed from the product and how it will withstand warpage and strain caused by temperature changes. Advanced packages that combine several chips in one package are also part of this role.

sections.h: Who they work with and what they handle
sections.p: They discuss pin placement and power delivery with chip designers, results of temperature cycling and other tests with reliability engineers, and final test methods with test engineers. They also often work with suppliers of materials such as package substrates and mold compounds, and with OSATs that provide assembly services. What they handle: materials such as lead frames, package substrates, solder balls, mold compound and underfill, plus assembly equipment, thermal and stress simulations, and inspection results from cross-sections and X-ray imaging.

This role draws on materials, mechanical, thermal and electrical knowledge all at once. The basics include stress caused by mismatched thermal expansion between materials, fatigue of solder and other joints, and estimating temperature rise from thermal resistance. For products with high-speed signals, electrical design knowledge about interconnect parasitics and signal quality is also needed. Some workplaces use simulation such as the finite element method. Advanced packaging also calls for knowledge of fine-pitch processing close to the front end, such as TSV (through-silicon via), redistribution layers (RDL) and hybrid bonding.

Start with the “Packaging and assembly” field to learn basic structures such as wire bonding, flip chip and BGA, and the assembly flow. Then cover the technologies that connect multiple chips in “Advanced packaging (3D and chiplets)”. Failure mechanisms that limit package lifetime are in “Reliability”, specifications such as thermal resistance and MSL are in “How to read datasheets”, and inspection after assembly is in “Testing and inspection”. The “Back end, quality and safety” course pulls the whole back end together.

faq.q: Can I become a packaging engineer without a technical background or industry experience?
faq.a: Knowledge of materials, mechanical or electrical engineering is useful for this role. Experience in nearby fields, such as electronics assembly, printed circuit boards or mechanical design, can be put to use. Policies on hiring and training people without industry experience differ by company and change over time, so check each job posting.

faq.q: How is it different from a front-end process engineer?
faq.a: Front-end process engineers handle the steps that build transistors and wiring on the wafer. Packaging engineers handle everything from cutting out the finished chip to turning it into a product, and their main themes are heat, mechanical strength and joining different materials. In advanced packaging, however, wiring and bonding are often done at the wafer level, so the boundary between the two is getting closer.

faq.q: Do I need any license or certification?
faq.a: In general, no specific license or certification is required. In practice, fundamentals of materials, thermal and mechanical engineering and experience with evaluation and simulation count most. Some people use skills certificates related to electronics assembly or soldering as study aids, but how much they count in hiring differs by company.

digital-design-engineer.name: Digital Design and Verification Engineer
digital-design-engineer.short: Engineers who design logic in a hardware description language, verify it by simulation and take it through logic synthesis and timing analysis to become a chip.
digital-design-engineer.description: What a digital design and verification engineer does: RTL design, testbenches and constrained random verification, synthesis and STA, plus the fields to study.

sections.p: Digital design engineers describe the functions of processors, communication circuits and other blocks at RTL (register-transfer level) using a hardware description language such as Verilog. Verification engineers check that the design behaves according to the specification, mainly through simulation with testbenches. On large chips, verification can take as much effort as design, or more. The RTL is converted into a gate-level circuit by logic synthesis, and STA (static timing analysis) checks that it runs at the target frequency. After place and route, tape-out, when the manufacturing data is handed off, marks the end of a cycle. Which stages an engineer covers depends on the company and the team.

sections.h: Who they work with and what they handle
sections.p: They work as a team with architects who define the specification, designers who integrate the whole chip, engineers responsible for place and route and timing, and DFT (design for testability) engineers who build in the test infrastructure. They may also discuss with software developers how to check behavior that the software on the chip will rely on. What they handle: specifications, RTL source code, testbenches, EDA tools, and simulation and timing analysis results. Design data is kept under version control just like software, and regression tests check the impact of each change.

The foundation is logic design basics: combinational and sequential circuits, flip-flops and state machines. On top of that, you need to tell apart synthesizable coding styles and verification coding styles in languages such as SystemVerilog. For timing, setup and hold time, slack and the handling of signals that cross between clock domains are important. For verification, learning constrained random verification and coverage concepts pays off. Automating work with scripting languages is also used widely.

Start with the “Logic circuits” field to build the basics, then learn how to write Verilog and how testbenches work in “HDL & Verification”. Next, cover the whole design flow in “IC design flow and EDA”, and timing and clock-crossing signals in “Timing analysis and CDC”. For processors, which are often the subject of design work, “CPUs and architecture” is useful. To prepare for job interviews, take the “Hardware interview prep” course; to study circuits and memory broadly, take “Circuits, design and memory”.

faq.q: Can I become a digital design or verification engineer without a technical background or industry experience?
faq.a: Logic design and programming knowledge are central to this role. In general, electrical, electronics or computing knowledge is usually expected, but some people come in through verification using their software development experience. Hiring requirements differ by company and change over time. Teaching yourself logic design and a hardware description language, then designing and simulating a small circuit, also helps you find out whether the work suits you.

faq.q: How is it different from a software engineer?
faq.a: A hardware description language looks like a programming language, but the big difference is that what you write becomes circuits that operate in parallel, not instructions executed one after another. Chips are also hard to fix after manufacturing, and a respin costs a lot of money and time, so verification before manufacturing is taken very seriously. Constantly keeping physical constraints such as timing, area and power in mind is another characteristic.

faq.q: Do I need any license or certification?
faq.a: In general, no specific license or certification is required. In practice, understanding logic design, hands-on experience designing or verifying with a hardware description language and a grasp of timing count most. As a student, running your own circuits on an FPGA lets you experience the flow from design to confirming that it works.

analog-design-engineer.name: Analog Design Engineer
analog-design-engineer.short: Engineers who design circuits that handle continuous voltages and currents, such as amplifiers, data converters and power circuits, with attention down to transistor characteristics and layout.
analog-design-engineer.description: What an analog design engineer does: analog and mixed-signal circuits, ADCs, DACs and power management, simulation and layout, plus the fields and terms to study.

sections.p: Analog design engineers design circuits such as amplifiers for sensor signals, ADCs and DACs that convert between analog signals and digital values, LDOs and DC-DC converters that generate supply voltages, and PLLs (phase-locked loops) that generate clocks. They often work on mixed-signal circuits combined with digital logic as well. They choose a circuit architecture from the specification, size the transistors and set bias currents, and use circuit simulation such as SPICE to check performance across temperature, supply voltage and manufacturing variation. They may also measure prototype chips to evaluate whether the performance matches the design.

sections.h: Who they work with and what they handle
sections.p: Analog performance depends heavily on layout, the placement of shapes on the chip, so they work closely with layout engineers. They also work with device engineers who provide the device models, digital designers who integrate the whole chip, the people who evaluate prototypes, and test engineers who build the production tests. What they handle: schematics, simulation results, device models including manufacturing variation (provided in the PDK), layouts and their verification results (DRC and LVS), and measurement data from prototypes.

The foundation includes MOSFET operation and small-signal models, op-amps and differential amplifiers, stability through negative feedback and phase margin, and noise. For ADCs and DACs you need to understand the sampling theorem, quantization and the trade-off between resolution and speed. The ability to sanity-check simulation results with hand calculations, rather than taking them at face value, is highly valued. Knowledge of layout, such as placing transistors symmetrically and being aware of parasitic capacitance and resistance, also reduces surprises at the prototype stage.

Start with the “Analog and electronic circuits” field to build the basics of op-amps, negative feedback and filters. Then learn converter architectures and how their performance is specified in “A/D and D/A conversion”, and transistor characteristics in “MOSFET”, so you can explain circuit behavior from the properties of the transistors. For the design flow and tools, “IC design flow and EDA” is useful; for power circuits, “Power semiconductors”; and for reading product specifications, “How to read datasheets”. Among the courses, “Circuits, design and memory” and “Understanding devices” are recommended.

faq.q: Can I become an analog design engineer without a technical background or industry experience?
faq.a: Analog design draws deeply on specialist knowledge of electronic circuits and devices, and in general an electrical or electronics background is usually expected. If you are starting without that experience, one possible path is to build experience in related work such as circuit evaluation or test first and move over later. Hiring requirements differ by company and change over time.

faq.q: How is it different from digital design?
faq.a: Digital circuits treat signals as 0s and 1s, and their design is highly automated with hardware description languages and EDA tools. Analog circuits handle continuous voltages and currents and are directly affected by noise, variation and temperature, so the designer more often decides the size and placement of individual transistors. Real chips use both together, so knowing the basics of the other side is valuable.

faq.q: Do I need any license or certification?
faq.a: In general, no specific license or certification is required. In practice, understanding of electronic circuits, experience designing with circuit simulation and experience confirming designs through measurement count most. As a student, designing a circuit in classes or research and checking it by simulation and measurement is good preparation.
